topic: dressing a floor loom, matching dye lots and darning a moth eaten wool blanket

provenance.author: CC (batch EN-1)
provenance.notes: napisane niezaleznie od korpusu PL, nie jest tlumaczeniem

base: I am dressing my floor loom for a blanket in wool and the warp keeps drifting sideways.
There is also a narrower loom by the window, which my aunt dressed and which behaves perfectly.
A digital scale sits on the bench, because I weigh every skein before winding it on.
The threads on the left half feel slack, while the right half sings under my finger.
Should I unwind the whole beam and start again, or can I correct this while weaving?
Unwind the beam, because uneven tension only worsens as more cloth rolls onto the front.
Slack threads take up weft differently and you will see a ridge across the finished blanket.
Wind on again with firm paper or sticks between the layers, keeping the pressure constant.
Only then is it worth judging the sett, because everything later rests on that beam.
I wound the warp on again with sticks and both halves now ring at the same pitch.
The narrower loom by the window has the same sticks, which explains a great deal now.
My trouble now is the wool itself, since two skeins came out darker from the dye pot.
Can I hide that difference in the weaving, or must I overdye the paler skeins?
Alternate the skeins every few picks and the eye will read the whole cloth as even.
Overdyeing is a blunt remedy, because it shifts every skein and rarely lands where you hoped.
Dye lots differ mostly through bath temperature and how crowded the pot was at the time.
Note the weight of wool against water next time and the lots will match far better.
Alternating the skeins worked and the darker wool has vanished into the surface of the cloth.
The narrower loom by the window is standing empty again, which frees my evenings nicely.
I have moved on to mending an older blanket that the moths reached last summer.
There are nine small holes, most of them no wider than a thumbnail across the weave.
I weighed the mending yarn on the digital scale, so the hem will not run short.
Should I darn each hole separately, or cut out the worst area and patch it wholesale?
Darn each hole separately, since a patch always pulls differently and shows at the corners.
Use yarn from the same fleece if you can, or unpick a hem for matching thread.
Work a small woven patch across each hole rather than pulling the edges tightly together.
Pulled edges gather the cloth and the mend then tears again along its own border.
I darned three holes with yarn unpicked from the hem and they lie almost flat.
The mended squares feel stiffer than the cloth around them, though the colour matches well.
The narrower loom is now free, so I could weave fresh cloth for the remaining holes.
Would woven patches sit better than darning, or does that create the same stiff squares?
Woven patches sit better on larger damage, but small holes are still best darned.
Stiffness usually comes from working the darn too tightly rather than from the yarn itself.
Leave a little slack in every pass, then press the mend under a damp cloth.
After washing the whole blanket once, the mends usually relax into the surrounding wool.
I washed the blanket gently and the darns have indeed softened into the surrounding wool.
The new blanket on the big loom is growing about a hand span each evening.
I am thinking about the finish now, since the edges curl slightly off the beam.
Is fulling in warm water enough, or should I press the whole thing under weight?
Full it gently in warm water first, because that is what stops the edges curling.
Agitate by hand for a few minutes only, then check the width against your measure.
Wool shrinks quickly once it decides to, and you cannot open the cloth again afterwards.
Dry it flat under a light board and the selvedges will stay straight for years.
